claims.text: Certain aluminum and other high-performance alloys are prone to hot cracking during conventional fusion welding.
The material's physical and microstructural characteristics cause hot cracking during conventional fusion welding.
Friction stir welding can join the damaged material in the solid state without reaching its melting temperature.
Friction stir processing induces severe plastic deformation in the repair region.
Friction stir processing induces dynamic recrystallization in the repair region.
Dynamic recrystallization during friction stir repair produces a fine-grained microstructure.
The fine-grained microstructure produced by friction stir repair has reduced susceptibility to hot cracking.
Melting and solidification during fusion welding enable hot cracking.
Friction stir repair circumvents hot-crack-generating melting and solidification stages.
Frictional heating and mechanical stirring promote formation of a solid-state joint.
Friction stir repair preserves the alloy's microstructure.
The friction stir repair mechanism enhances mechanical integrity under stress.
Friction stir repair will produce fewer or no hot cracks relative to traditional fusion-welded repair.
Friction stir repair will produce a more refined grain structure than traditional fusion-welded repair.
Friction stir repair will improve fatigue performance relative to traditional fusion-welded repair.
Friction stir repair will improve thermal performance relative to traditional fusion-welded repair.
Traditional fusion-welding repair results in hot cracking and compromised microstructural integrity in the target material.
Friction stir welding has shown promise for mitigating hot cracking in similar alloys.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator says friction stir repair substantially transforms the microstructure through severe plastic deformation, dynamic recrystallization, and grain refinement, whereas the mechanism says that it preserves the alloy's microstructure.
